ROAD TRANSPORT (WORKING TIME) REGULATIONS 
The Road Transport (Working Time) Regulations (RTWT) requires employment businesses to 
maintain records of the Working Time of mobile workers who are involved in operations subject to 
EU drivers’ hour’s rules.  An employment business is obliged to ensure that the Working Time limits

• 
Mobile drivers (such as HGV drivers and crew) are subject to a maximum average Working 
Time of 48 hours per week over a default 17 week reference period; this default reference period 
may be changed to a rolling reference period and extended to 26 weeks in certain circumstances. 
• 
There is a maximum weekly limit of 60 hours Working Time. 
• 
There is a maximum of 10 hours night work within each 24 hour period.  Night time is 
defined as midnight to 0400 hours (for goods vehicles) and 0100 and 0500 hours (for passenger 
vehicles).  This maximum may be extended in certain circumstances. 
• 
Rest periods – mobile workers MUST take the following breaks:  30 minutes after 6 hours 
Working Time and 45 minutes for over 9 hours Working Time.  It is important to note that EU Drivers 
Hours breaks and rest periods still apply.

26 week calendar reference period.  The reference period we will use begins on midnight on the 
nearest Monday on or after 1 April, 1 August and 1 December each year and ending at midnight at 
the beginning of the nearest Monday falling on or after 26 weeks of these dates. Accordingly the 
reference periods are as follows: PERIOD 1 = 1ST JANUARY TO 30TH JUNE   [26 WEEKS] PERIOD 2 = 
1ST JULY TO 31ST DECEMBER  [26 WEEKS] 
First Call Contract Services operates a 26 week rolling reference period.

your responsibility to accurately record your Working Time during an Assignment. RTWT Regulations 
have been introduced to protect and safeguard the health and safety of mobile workers, other road 
users and the public.  A mobile worker also has a responsibility for complying with the Regulations.

If the mobile worker knowingly breaks the rules (e.g. neglects to inform his employer or employment

According to the working-time declaration, what is the maximum average weekly working time for mobile drivers?

answer:
The maximum average weekly working time for mobile drivers, as specified by the RTWT Regulations, is 48 hours over a 26-week reference period. This can be broken down as follows:

- A default 17-week reference period is used initially.
- This can be changed to a rolling 26-week reference period in certain circumstances.

Additionally, there is a maximum weekly limit of 60 hours of Working Time.

Process
[edit]Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enhances large language models (LLMs) by incorporating an information-retrieval mechanism that allows models to access and utilize additional data beyond their original training set. Ars Technica notes that "when new information becomes available, rather than having to retrain the model, all that's needed is to augment the model's external knowledge base with the updated information ("augmentation").[5] IBM states that "in the generative phase, the LLM draws from the augmented prompt and its internal representation of its training data to synthesize" an answer.[1]
RAG key stages
[edit]Typically, the data to be referenced is converted into LLM embeddings, numerical representations in the form of a large vector space. RAG can be used on unstructured (usually text), semi-structured, or structured data (for example knowledge graphs). These embeddings are then stored in a vector database to allow for document retrieval.
Given a user query, a document retriever is first called to select the most relevant documents that will be used to augment the query.[3][4] This comparison can be done using a variety of methods, which depend in part on the type of indexing used.[1]

---

Source marker: [Web - Retrieval-augmented generation - Wikipedia]
Retrieval-augmented generation
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a technique that enables large language models (LLMs) to retrieve and incorporate new information from external data sources.[1][2] With RAG, LLMs first refer to a specified set of documents, then respond to user queries. These documents supplement information from the LLM's pre-existing training data.[3] This allows LLMs to use domain-specific and/or updated information that is not available in the training data.[3] For example, this enables LLM-based chatbots to access internal company data or generate responses based on authoritative sources. The technique was first proposed in 2020 and has since become a widely adopted approach in modern AI systems.
RAG improves LLMs by incorporating information retrieval before generating responses.[4] Unlike LLMs that rely on static training data, RAG pulls relevant text from databases, uploaded documents, or web sources.[1] According to Ars Technica, "RAG is a way of improving LLM performance, in essence by blending the LLM process with a web search or other document look-up process to help LLMs stick to the facts." This method helps reduce AI hallucinations,[4] which have caused chatbots to describe policies that don't exist, or recommend nonexistent legal cases to lawyers that are looking for citations to support their arguments.[5]

Source marker: [Web - Retrieval-augmented generation - Wikipedia]
RAG also reduces the need to retrain LLMs with new data, saving on computational and financial costs.[1] Beyond efficiency gains, RAG also allows LLMs to include sources in their responses, so users can verify the cited sources. This provides greater transparency, as users can cross-check retrieved content to ensure accuracy and relevance.
The term retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) was introduced in a 2020 paper that described combining a parametric language model with a non-parametric external memory accessed through retrieval at inference time.[4]

Retriever-centric methods
[edit]These methods aim to enhance the quality of document retrieval in vector databases:
- Pre-training the retriever using the Inverse Cloze Task (ICT), a technique that helps the model learn retrieval patterns by predicting masked text within documents.[13]
- Supervised retriever optimization aligns retrieval probabilities with the generator model's likelihood distribution. This involves retrieving the top-k vectors for a given prompt, scoring the generated response's perplexity, and minimizing KL divergence between the retriever's selections and the model's likelihoods to refine retrieval.[14]
- Reranking techniques can refine retriever performance by prioritizing the most relevant retrieved documents during training.[15]
Language model
[edit]By redesigning the language model with the retriever in mind, a 25-time smaller network can get comparable perplexity as its much larger counterparts.[16] Because it is trained from scratch, this method (Retro) incurs the high cost of training runs that the original RAG scheme avoided. The hypothesis is that by giving domain knowledge during training, Retro needs less focus on the domain and can devote its smaller weight resources only to language semantics. While RAG improves the accuracy of large language models (LLMs), it does not eliminate all challenges. One limitation is that while RAG reduces the need for frequent model retraining, it does not remove it entirely. Additionally, LLMs may struggle to recognize when they lack sufficient information to provide a reliable response. Without specific training, models may generate answers even when they should indicate uncertainty. According to IBM, this issue can arise when the model lacks the ability to assess its own knowledge limitations.[1]
RAG poisoning
[edit]RAG systems may retrieve factually correct but misleading sources, leading to errors in interpretation. In some cases, an LLM may extract statements from a source without considering its context, resulting in an incorrect conclusion. Additionally, when faced with conflicting information, RAG models may struggle to determine which source is accurate. The worst case outcome of this limitation is that the model may combine details from multiple sources producing responses that merge outdated and updated information in a misleading manner. According to the MIT Technology Review, these issues occur because RAG systems may misinterpret the data they retrieve.[3]

- **Use Updated Information:** RAG enables the model to draw on recent or domain-specific information that wasn't included in its initial training. For instance, it can reference internal company data or authoritative sources.
  
- **Reduce Hallucinations:** By integrating real-world data, RAG helps reduce instances where the model generates false or nonsensical information (hallucinations).

- **Enhance Accuracy and Relevance:** The model can provide more accurate and relevant responses by grounding its outputs in external data, which can include medical knowledge, legal references, or other specialized information.

- **Avoid Retraining:** RAG minimizes the need for frequent retraining of the model with new data, saving computational and financial resources.

- **Provide Source Verification:** Users can verify the sources cited in the model’s responses, enhancing transparency and trust.

This integration of external data significantly improves the model's utility across various applications, particularly in scenarios requiring up-to-date or specialized information.

RAG and LLM limitations
[edit]LLMs can provide incorrect information. For example, when Google first demonstrated its LLM tool "Bard" (later re-branded to Google Gemini), the LLM provided incorrect information about the James Webb Space Telescope. This error contributed to a $100 billion decline in Google's stock value.[5] RAG is used to prevent these errors, but it does not solve all the problems. For example, LLMs can generate misinformation even when pulling from factually correct sources if they misinterpret the context. MIT Technology Review gives the example of an AI-generated response stating, "The United States has had one Muslim president, Barack Hussein Obama." The model retrieved this from the rhetorical chapter title "Barack Hussein Obama: America's First Muslim President?" in the book Faith in the New Millennium: The Future of Religion and American Politics.[6] The LLM did not "know" or "understand" the context of the title, generating a false statement.[3]
LLMs with RAG are programmed to prioritize new information. This technique has been called "prompt stuffing." Without prompt stuffing, the LLM's input is generated by a user; with prompt stuffing, additional relevant context is added to this input to guide the model's response. This approach provides the LLM with key information early in the prompt, encouraging it to prioritize the supplied data over pre-existing training knowledge.[7]

How can a RAG system use new information without retraining the language model?

answer:
A RAG system can use new information without retraining the language model by augmenting the model's external knowledge base. Here’s how it works:

- **External Knowledge Base Augmentation**: When new information becomes available, instead of retraining the entire model, the RAG system updates the external knowledge base. This means adding or modifying the documents and data that the model can reference.

- **Prompt Engineering**: The system feeds the relevant retrieved information into the language model via prompt engineering of the user's original query. This ensures that the model uses the latest information without needing to be retrained.

- **Document Retrieval**: The RAG system retrieves the most relevant documents for a given query. These documents are then used to augment the query, providing the model with context and information that might not be present in its original training data.

- **Synthesis of Information**: During the generative phase, the language model synthesizes an answer using both the augmented prompt and its internal representation of the training data. This allows the model to incorporate new information seamlessly.

This approach leverages the existing model architecture while dynamically updating it with new data, thus enhancing its capabilities without the need for extensive retraining.

Retrieval-augmented generation
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a technique that enables large language models (LLMs) to retrieve and incorporate new information from external data sources.[1][2] With RAG, LLMs first refer to a specified set of documents, then respond to user queries. These documents supplement information from the LLM's pre-existing training data.[3] This allows LLMs to use domain-specific and/or updated information that is not available in the training data.[3] For example, this enables LLM-based chatbots to access internal company data or generate responses based on authoritative sources. The technique was first proposed in 2020 and has since become a widely adopted approach in modern AI systems.
RAG improves LLMs by incorporating information retrieval before generating responses.[4] Unlike LLMs that rely on static training data, RAG pulls relevant text from databases, uploaded documents, or web sources.[1] According to Ars Technica, "RAG is a way of improving LLM performance, in essence by blending the LLM process with a web search or other document look-up process to help LLMs stick to the facts." This method helps reduce AI hallucinations,[4] which have caused chatbots to describe policies that don't exist, or recommend nonexistent legal cases to lawyers that are looking for citations to support their arguments.[5]

Source marker: [Web - Retrieval-augmented generation - Wikipedia]
The model feeds this relevant retrieved information into the LLM via prompt engineering of the user's original query. Newer implementations (as of 2023[update]) can also incorporate specific augmentation modules with abilities such as expanding queries into multiple domains and using memory and self-improvement to learn from previous retrievals.[citation needed]
Finally, the LLM can generate output based on both the query and the retrieved documents.[3][4] Some models incorporate extra steps to improve output, such as the re-ranking of retrieved information, context selection, and fine-tuning.
Applications
[edit]Retrieval-augmented generation is used in applications where generated responses need to be grounded in external or frequently updated information.[citation needed]
In healthcare, RAG has been studied as a way to ground large language model outputs in external medical knowledge sources, although reviews have noted continuing challenges around evaluation, ethics, and clinical reliability.[8]

Source marker: [Web - Retrieval-augmented generation - Wikipedia]
RAG and LLM limitations
[edit]LLMs can provide incorrect information. For example, when Google first demonstrated its LLM tool "Bard" (later re-branded to Google Gemini), the LLM provided incorrect information about the James Webb Space Telescope. This error contributed to a $100 billion decline in Google's stock value.[5] RAG is used to prevent these errors, but it does not solve all the problems. For example, LLMs can generate misinformation even when pulling from factually correct sources if they misinterpret the context. MIT Technology Review gives the example of an AI-generated response stating, "The United States has had one Muslim president, Barack Hussein Obama." The model retrieved this from the rhetorical chapter title "Barack Hussein Obama: America's First Muslim President?" in the book Faith in the New Millennium: The Future of Religion and American Politics.[6] The LLM did not "know" or "understand" the context of the title, generating a false statement.[3]
LLMs with RAG are programmed to prioritize new information. This technique has been called "prompt stuffing." Without prompt stuffing, the LLM's input is generated by a user; with prompt stuffing, additional relevant context is added to this input to guide the model's response. This approach provides the LLM with key information early in the prompt, encouraging it to prioritize the supplied data over pre-existing training knowledge.[7]

Chunking
[edit]Chunking involves various strategies for breaking up the data into vectors so the retriever can find details in it.
Hybrid search
[edit]Sometimes vector database searches (aka semantic search technique) can miss key facts needed to answer a user's question. One way to mitigate this is to do a traditional text search (aka full text search), combine those results to the text chunks linked to the retrieved vectors from the vector search, and feed the combined hybrid text (using effective scoring or reranking scoring) into the language model for generation.[18]
Challenges
[edit]RAG does not prevent hallucinations in LLMs. According to Ars Technica, "It is not a direct solution because the LLM can still hallucinate around the source material in its response."[5]

Retriever-centric methods
[edit]These methods aim to enhance the quality of document retrieval in vector databases:
- Pre-training the retriever using the Inverse Cloze Task (ICT), a technique that helps the model learn retrieval patterns by predicting masked text within documents.[13]
- Supervised retriever optimization aligns retrieval probabilities with the generator model's likelihood distribution. This involves retrieving the top-k vectors for a given prompt, scoring the generated response's perplexity, and minimizing KL divergence between the retriever's selections and the model's likelihoods to refine retrieval.[14]
- Reranking techniques can refine retriever performance by prioritizing the most relevant retrieved documents during training.[15]
Language model
[edit]By redesigning the language model with the retriever in mind, a 25-time smaller network can get comparable perplexity as its much larger counterparts.[16] Because it is trained from scratch, this method (Retro) incurs the high cost of training runs that the original RAG scheme avoided. The hypothesis is that by giving domain knowledge during training, Retro needs less focus on the domain and can devote its smaller weight resources only to language semantics. Retrieval-augmented generation
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a technique that enables large language models (LLMs) to retrieve and incorporate new information from external data sources.[1][2] With RAG, LLMs first refer to a specified set of documents, then respond to user queries. These documents supplement information from the LLM's pre-existing training data.[3] This allows LLMs to use domain-specific and/or updated information that is not available in the training data.[3] For example, this enables LLM-based chatbots to access internal company data or generate responses based on authoritative sources. The technique was first proposed in 2020 and has since become a widely adopted approach in modern AI systems.
RAG improves LLMs by incorporating information retrieval before generating responses.[4] Unlike LLMs that rely on static training data, RAG pulls relevant text from databases, uploaded documents, or web sources.[1] According to Ars Technica, "RAG is a way of improving LLM performance, in essence by blending the LLM process with a web search or other document look-up process to help LLMs stick to the facts." This method helps reduce AI hallucinations,[4] which have caused chatbots to describe policies that don't exist, or recommend nonexistent legal cases to lawyers that are looking for citations to support their arguments.[5]

Retriever-centric methods
[edit]These methods aim to enhance the quality of document retrieval in vector databases:
- Pre-training the retriever using the Inverse Cloze Task (ICT), a technique that helps the model learn retrieval patterns by predicting masked text within documents.[13]
- Supervised retriever optimization aligns retrieval probabilities with the generator model's likelihood distribution. This involves retrieving the top-k vectors for a given prompt, scoring the generated response's perplexity, and minimizing KL divergence between the retriever's selections and the model's likelihoods to refine retrieval.[14]
- Reranking techniques can refine retriever performance by prioritizing the most relevant retrieved documents during training.[15]

[edit]By redesigning the language model with the retriever in mind, a 25-time smaller network can get comparable perplexity as its much larger counterparts.[16] Because it is trained from scratch, this method (Retro) incurs the high cost of training runs that the original RAG scheme avoided. The hypothesis is that by giving domain knowledge during training, Retro needs less focus on the domain and can devote its smaller weight resources only to language semantics. How does the retriever select documents before the LLM generates an answer?

answer:
The retriever selects documents before the LLM generates an answer through several steps:

1. **Conversion to Embeddings**: The data to be referenced is first converted into embeddings, which are numerical representations in the form of large vectors.

2. **Storage in Vector Database**: These embeddings are then stored in a vector database to facilitate efficient document retrieval.

3. **Document Retrieval**: Given a user query, a document retriever is called to select the most relevant documents. This selection can be done using various methods depending on the type of indexing used.

4. **Relevance Comparison**: The retriever compares the query with the stored embeddings to identify the most relevant documents. Methods for this comparison include:
   - **Inverse Cloze Task (ICT)**: Helps the model learn retrieval patterns by predicting masked text within documents.
   - **Supervised Retriever Optimization**: Aligns retrieval probabilities with the generator model's likelihood distribution.
   - **Reranking Techniques**: Prioritize the most relevant retrieved documents during training.

5. **Prompt Engineering**: The relevant retrieved information is then fed into the LLM via prompt engineering of the user's original query.

This process ensures that the LLM has access to the most pertinent information before generating a response, enhancing the accuracy and relevance of the output.

Does RAG completely prevent a language model from hallucinating?

answer:
No, RAG does not completely prevent a language model from hallucinating. While RAG improves the accuracy of large language models (LLMs) by allowing them to access and utilize additional data, it still faces several limitations:

- **Hallucination Risk**: RAG does not eliminate the risk of hallucinations. LLMs can still generate information that is not aligned with the source material or factual inaccuracies, even when using RAG.
- **Context Misinterpretation**: LLMs may misinterpret the context of retrieved information, leading to incorrect conclusions.
- **Combining Outdated and Updated Information**: RAG models might merge outdated and updated information in a misleading manner, especially when dealing with conflicting sources.
- **Model Uncertainty**: LLMs may struggle to recognize when they lack sufficient information to provide a reliable response, leading to the generation of answers even when the model should indicate uncertainty.

These issues highlight that while RAG is a valuable tool for enhancing the performance of LLMs, it does not fully address the challenge of hallucinations.

Process
[edit]Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enhances large language models (LLMs) by incorporating an information-retrieval mechanism that allows models to access and utilize additional data beyond their original training set. Ars Technica notes that "when new information becomes available, rather than having to retrain the model, all that's needed is to augment the model's external knowledge base with the updated information ("augmentation").[5] IBM states that "in the generative phase, the LLM draws from the augmented prompt and its internal representation of its training data to synthesize" an answer.[1]
RAG key stages
[edit]Typically, the data to be referenced is converted into LLM embeddings, numerical representations in the form of a large vector space. RAG can be used on unstructured (usually text), semi-structured, or structured data (for example knowledge graphs). These embeddings are then stored in a vector database to allow for document retrieval.
Given a user query, a document retriever is first called to select the most relevant documents that will be used to augment the query.[3][4] This comparison can be done using a variety of methods, which depend in part on the type of indexing used.[1]

---

Source marker: [Web - Retrieval-augmented generation - Wikipedia]
RAG and LLM limitations
[edit]LLMs can provide incorrect information. For example, when Google first demonstrated its LLM tool "Bard" (later re-branded to Google Gemini), the LLM provided incorrect information about the James Webb Space Telescope. This error contributed to a $100 billion decline in Google's stock value.[5] RAG is used to prevent these errors, but it does not solve all the problems. For example, LLMs can generate misinformation even when pulling from factually correct sources if they misinterpret the context. MIT Technology Review gives the example of an AI-generated response stating, "The United States has had one Muslim president, Barack Hussein Obama." The model retrieved this from the rhetorical chapter title "Barack Hussein Obama: America's First Muslim President?" in the book Faith in the New Millennium: The Future of Religion and American Politics.[6] The LLM did not "know" or "understand" the context of the title, generating a false statement.[3]
LLMs with RAG are programmed to prioritize new information. This technique has been called "prompt stuffing." Without prompt stuffing, the LLM's input is generated by a user; with prompt stuffing, additional relevant context is added to this input to guide the model's response. This approach provides the LLM with key information early in the prompt, encouraging it to prioritize the supplied data over pre-existing training knowledge.[7]

This provides greater transparency, as users can cross-check retrieved content to ensure accuracy and relevance.
The term retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) was introduced in a 2020 paper that described combining a parametric language model with a non-parametric external memory accessed through retrieval at inference time.[4]

Source marker: [Web - Retrieval-augmented generation - Wikipedia]
Retrieval-augmented generation
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a technique that enables large language models (LLMs) to retrieve and incorporate new information from external data sources.[1][2] With RAG, LLMs first refer to a specified set of documents, then respond to user queries. These documents supplement information from the LLM's pre-existing training data.[3] This allows LLMs to use domain-specific and/or updated information that is not available in the training data.[3] For example, this enables LLM-based chatbots to access internal company data or generate responses based on authoritative sources. The technique was first proposed in 2020 and has since become a widely adopted approach in modern AI systems.
RAG improves LLMs by incorporating information retrieval before generating responses.[4] Unlike LLMs that rely on static training data, RAG pulls relevant text from databases, uploaded documents, or web sources.[1] According to Ars Technica, "RAG is a way of improving LLM performance, in essence by blending the LLM process with a web search or other document look-up process to help LLMs stick to the facts." This method helps reduce AI hallucinations,[4] which have caused chatbots to describe policies that don't exist, or recommend nonexistent legal cases to lawyers that are looking for citations to support their arguments.[5]
How does hybrid search compensate when semantic search misses key facts?

answer:
Hybrid search compensates when semantic search misses key facts by combining vector database searches with traditional text searches. Here’s how it works:

- **Vector Database Search**: This uses semantic search techniques to find similar documents based on the meaning of the query.
- **Traditional Text Search**: This performs a full-text search to find exact matches or closely related phrases that might be missed by the vector search.
- **Combining Results**: The results from both types of searches are combined and fed into the language model for generation. This hybrid approach ensures that no critical information is overlooked.

This combination enhances the comprehensiveness and accuracy of the search results, making the overall system more robust in handling complex queries.

Process
[edit]Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enhances large language models (LLMs) by incorporating an information-retrieval mechanism that allows models to access and utilize additional data beyond their original training set. Ars Technica notes that "when new information becomes available, rather than having to retrain the model, all that's needed is to augment the model's external knowledge base with the updated information ("augmentation").[5] IBM states that "in the generative phase, the LLM draws from the augmented prompt and its internal representation of its training data to synthesize" an answer.[1]
RAG key stages
[edit]Typically, the data to be referenced is converted into LLM embeddings, numerical representations in the form of a large vector space. RAG can be used on unstructured (usually text), semi-structured, or structured data (for example knowledge graphs). These embeddings are then stored in a vector database to allow for document retrieval.
Given a user query, a document retriever is first called to select the most relevant documents that will be used to augment the query.[3][4] This comparison can be done using a variety of methods, which depend in part on the type of indexing used.[1]

Hybrid search
[edit]Sometimes vector database searches (aka semantic search technique) can miss key facts needed to answer a user's question. Retrieval-augmented generation
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a technique that enables large language models (LLMs) to retrieve and incorporate new information from external data sources.[1][2] With RAG, LLMs first refer to a specified set of documents, then respond to user queries. These documents supplement information from the LLM's pre-existing training data.[3] This allows LLMs to use domain-specific and/or updated information that is not available in the training data.[3] For example, this enables LLM-based chatbots to access internal company data or generate responses based on authoritative sources. The technique was first proposed in 2020 and has since become a widely adopted approach in modern AI systems.
RAG improves LLMs by incorporating information retrieval before generating responses.[4] Unlike LLMs that rely on static training data, RAG pulls relevant text from databases, uploaded documents, or web sources.[1] According to Ars Technica, "RAG is a way of improving LLM performance, in essence by blending the LLM process with a web search or other document look-up process to help LLMs stick to the facts." This method helps reduce AI hallucinations,[4] which have caused chatbots to describe policies that don't exist, or recommend nonexistent legal cases to lawyers that are looking for citations to support their arguments.[5]
What pre-training task teaches a retriever to predict masked text?

answer: The pre-training task that teaches a retriever to predict masked text is the Inverse Cloze Task (ICT). This technique helps the model learn retrieval patterns by predicting masked text within documents, enhancing its ability to understand and retrieve relevant information.

According to IBM, this issue can arise when the model lacks the ability to assess its own knowledge limitations.[1]
RAG poisoning
[edit]RAG systems may retrieve factually correct but misleading sources, leading to errors in interpretation. In some cases, an LLM may extract statements from a source without considering its context, resulting in an incorrect conclusion. Additionally, when faced with conflicting information, RAG models may struggle to determine which source is accurate. The worst case outcome of this limitation is that the model may combine details from multiple sources producing responses that merge outdated and updated information in a misleading manner. According to the MIT Technology Review, these issues occur because RAG systems may misinterpret the data they retrieve.[3]

[edit]These methods focus on the encoding of text as either dense or sparse vectors. Sparse vectors, which encode the identity of a word, are typically dictionary-length and contain mostly zeros. - Hybrid vector approaches may be used to combine dense vector representations with sparse one-hot vectors, taking advantage of the computational efficiency of sparse dot products over dense vector operations.[9]

Retrieval-augmented generation
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a technique that enables large language models (LLMs) to retrieve and incorporate new information from external data sources.[1][2] With RAG, LLMs first refer to a specified set of documents, then respond to user queries. These documents supplement information from the LLM's pre-existing training data.[3] This allows LLMs to use domain-specific and/or updated information that is not available in the training data.[3] For example, this enables LLM-based chatbots to access internal company data or generate responses based on authoritative sources. The technique was first proposed in 2020 and has since become a widely adopted approach in modern AI systems.
RAG improves LLMs by incorporating information retrieval before generating responses.[4] Unlike LLMs that rely on static training data, RAG pulls relevant text from databases, uploaded documents, or web sources.[1] According to Ars Technica, "RAG is a way of improving LLM performance, in essence by blending the LLM process with a web search or other document look-up process to help LLMs stick to the facts." This method helps reduce AI hallucinations,[4] which have caused chatbots to describe policies that don't exist, or recommend nonexistent legal cases to lawyers that are looking for citations to support their arguments.[5]

---

Source marker: [Web - Retrieval-augmented generation - Wikipedia]
RAG and LLM limitations
[edit]LLMs can provide incorrect information. For example, when Google first demonstrated its LLM tool "Bard" (later re-branded to Google Gemini), the LLM provided incorrect information about the James Webb Space Telescope. This error contributed to a $100 billion decline in Google's stock value.[5] RAG is used to prevent these errors, but it does not solve all the problems. For example, LLMs can generate misinformation even when pulling from factually correct sources if they misinterpret the context. MIT Technology Review gives the example of an AI-generated response stating, "The United States has had one Muslim president, Barack Hussein Obama." The model retrieved this from the rhetorical chapter title "Barack Hussein Obama: America's First Muslim President?" in the book Faith in the New Millennium: The Future of Religion and American Politics.[6] The LLM did not "know" or "understand" the context of the title, generating a false statement.[3]
LLMs with RAG are programmed to prioritize new information. This technique has been called "prompt stuffing." Without prompt stuffing, the LLM's input is generated by a user; with prompt stuffing, additional relevant context is added to this input to guide the model's response. This approach provides the LLM with key information early in the prompt, encouraging it to prioritize the supplied data over pre-existing training knowledge.[7]

These documents supplement information from the LLM's pre-existing training data.[3] This allows LLMs to use domain-specific and/or updated information that is not available in the training data.[3] For example, this enables LLM-based chatbots to access internal company data or generate responses based on authoritative sources. The technique was first proposed in 2020 and has since become a widely adopted approach in modern AI systems.
RAG improves LLMs by incorporating information retrieval before generating responses.[4] Unlike LLMs that rely on static training data, RAG pulls relevant text from databases, uploaded documents, or web sources.[1] According to Ars Technica, "RAG is a way of improving LLM performance, in essence by blending the LLM process with a web search or other document look-up process to help LLMs stick to the facts." This method helps reduce AI hallucinations,[4] which have caused chatbots to describe policies that don't exist, or recommend nonexistent legal cases to lawyers that are looking for citations to support their arguments.[5]

The model feeds this relevant retrieved information into the LLM via prompt engineering of the user's original query. Newer implementations (as of 2023[update]) can also incorporate specific augmentation modules with abilities such as expanding queries into multiple domains and using memory and self-improvement to learn from previous retrievals.[citation needed]
Finally, the LLM can generate output based on both the query and the retrieved documents.[3][4] Some models incorporate extra steps to improve output, such as the re-ranking of retrieved information, context selection, and fine-tuning.
Applications
[edit]Retrieval-augmented generation is used in applications where generated responses need to be grounded in external or frequently updated information.[citation needed]
In healthcare, RAG has been studied as a way to ground large language model outputs in external medical knowledge sources, although reviews have noted continuing challenges around evaluation, ethics, and clinical reliability.[8]

Process
[edit]Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enhances large language models (LLMs) by incorporating an information-retrieval mechanism that allows models to access and utilize additional data beyond their original training set. Ars Technica notes that "when new information becomes available, rather than having to retrain the model, all that's needed is to augment the model's external knowledge base with the updated information ("augmentation").[5] IBM states that "in the generative phase, the LLM draws from the augmented prompt and its internal representation of its training data to synthesize" an answer.[1]
RAG key stages
[edit]Typically, the data to be referenced is converted into LLM embeddings, numerical representations in the form of a large vector space. RAG can be used on unstructured (usually text), semi-structured, or structured data (for example knowledge graphs). These embeddings are then stored in a vector database to allow for document retrieval.
Given a user query, a document retriever is first called to select the most relevant documents that will be used to augment the query.[3][4] This comparison can be done using a variety of methods, which depend in part on the type of indexing used.[1]

---

Source marker: [Web - Retrieval-augmented generation - Wikipedia]
Retriever-centric methods
[edit]These methods aim to enhance the quality of document retrieval in vector databases:
- Pre-training the retriever using the Inverse Cloze Task (ICT), a technique that helps the model learn retrieval patterns by predicting masked text within documents.[13]
- Supervised retriever optimization aligns retrieval probabilities with the generator model's likelihood distribution. This involves retrieving the top-k vectors for a given prompt, scoring the generated response's perplexity, and minimizing KL divergence between the retriever's selections and the model's likelihoods to refine retrieval.[14]
- Reranking techniques can refine retriever performance by prioritizing the most relevant retrieved documents during training.[15]
Language model
[edit]By redesigning the language model with the retriever in mind, a 25-time smaller network can get comparable perplexity as its much larger counterparts.[16] Because it is trained from scratch, this method (Retro) incurs the high cost of training runs that the original RAG scheme avoided. The hypothesis is that by giving domain knowledge during training, Retro needs less focus on the domain and can devote its smaller weight resources only to language semantics. The redesigned language model is shown here.
It has been reported that Retro is not reproducible, so modifications were made to make it so. The more reproducible version is called Retro++ and includes in-context RAG.[17]

RAG poisoning
[edit]RAG systems may retrieve factually correct but misleading sources, leading to errors in interpretation. In some cases, an LLM may extract statements from a source without considering its context, resulting in an incorrect conclusion. Additionally, when faced with conflicting information, RAG models may struggle to determine which source is accurate. The worst case outcome of this limitation is that the model may combine details from multiple sources producing responses that merge outdated and updated information in a misleading manner. According to the MIT Technology Review, these issues occur because RAG systems may misinterpret the data they retrieve.[3]

[edit]Chunking involves various strategies for breaking up the data into vectors so the retriever can find details in it.
Hybrid search
[edit]Sometimes vector database searches (aka semantic search technique) can miss key facts needed to answer a user's question. One way to mitigate this is to do a traditional text search (aka full text search), combine those results to the text chunks linked to the retrieved vectors from the vector search, and feed the combined hybrid text (using effective scoring or reranking scoring) into the language model for generation.[18]

RAG and LLM limitations
[edit]LLMs can provide incorrect information. For example, when Google first demonstrated its LLM tool "Bard" (later re-branded to Google Gemini), the LLM provided incorrect information about the James Webb Space Telescope. This error contributed to a $100 billion decline in Google's stock value.[5] RAG is used to prevent these errors, but it does not solve all the problems. For example, LLMs can generate misinformation even when pulling from factually correct sources if they misinterpret the context. MIT Technology Review gives the example of an AI-generated response stating, "The United States has had one Muslim president, Barack Hussein Obama." The model retrieved this from the rhetorical chapter title "Barack Hussein Obama: America's First Muslim President?" in the book Faith in the New Millennium: The Future of Religion and American Politics.[6] The LLM did not "know" or "understand" the context of the title, generating a false statement.[3]
LLMs with RAG are programmed to prioritize new information. This technique has been called "prompt stuffing." Without prompt stuffing, the LLM's input is generated by a user; with prompt stuffing, additional relevant context is added to this input to guide the model's response. This approach provides the LLM with key information early in the prompt, encouraging it to prioritize the supplied data over pre-existing training knowledge.[7]

Can a model still answer incorrectly when RAG retrieves factually correct material, and why?

expected_facts: Yes. The model can misinterpret the context even when retrieved sources are factually correct.
answer:
Yes, a model can still answer incorrectly even when RAG retrieves factually correct material. This occurs due to several reasons:

- **Misinterpretation of Context**: The model might extract statements from a source without fully understanding the context, leading to incorrect conclusions. For instance, it could take a title or phrase out of context, as seen in the example where the model generated a false statement about Barack Obama being the first Muslim president.

- **Combining Outdated and Updated Information**: When faced with conflicting information, the model might blend outdated and updated data in a misleading manner, creating a false synthesis.

- **Lack of Self-Awareness**: Models may struggle to recognize when they lack sufficient information to provide a reliable response. Even with RAG, they might generate answers based on insufficient or incomplete data, leading to inaccuracies.

- **Prompt Stuffing Limitations**: While RAG can help by providing relevant context early in the prompt, the model might still prioritize this new information over its existing knowledge, potentially leading to misinformation if the new information is incorrect or misleading.

These issues highlight the ongoing challenges in ensuring the accuracy and reliability of AI-generated responses, despite the benefits of RAG in integrating external data.

Summary of the RTWT Regulations:

- **Working Time Limits:** Mobile drivers must not exceed an average of 48 hours per week over a 26-week reference period, which can be adjusted to a rolling 26-week period. There is a maximum of 60 hours of Working Time per week. Night work is limited to 10 hours within any 24-hour period, defined as midnight to 0400 hours for goods vehicles and 0100 to 0500 hours for passenger vehicles. These limits can be extended in certain circumstances.

- **Breaks:** Workers must take a 30-minute break after 6 hours of Working Time and a 45-minute break after 9 hours of Working Time. EU drivers' hours rules and rest periods still apply.

- **Reference Periods:** The reference period is a 26-week calendar period starting from the nearest Monday on or after 1 April, 1 August, and 1 December, ending at midnight on the nearest Monday after 26 weeks. This results in two 26-week periods per year: Period 1 (January to June) and Period 2 (July to December).

- **Worker Responsibilities:** Workers must inform their employer or employment business of all Working Time during the reference periods and update them about any additional Working Time for other employers. Accurate recording of Working Time is essential. Failure to comply with these regulations can result in a criminal offense, with a potential fine of up to £5,000. All work, whether transport or non-transport, must be declared, including charitable or voluntary work, even if it is excluded from the Working Time calculation.

Process
[edit]Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enhances large language models (LLMs) by incorporating an information-retrieval mechanism that allows models to access and utilize additional data beyond their original training set. Ars Technica notes that "when new information becomes available, rather than having to retrain the model, all that's needed is to augment the model's external knowledge base with the updated information ("augmentation").[5] IBM states that "in the generative phase, the LLM draws from the augmented prompt and its internal representation of its training data to synthesize" an answer.[1]
RAG key stages
[edit]Typically, the data to be referenced is converted into LLM embeddings, numerical representations in the form of a large vector space. RAG can be used on unstructured (usually text), semi-structured, or structured data (for example knowledge graphs). These embeddings are then stored in a vector database to allow for document retrieval.
Given a user query, a document retriever is first called to select the most relevant documents that will be used to augment the query.[3][4] This comparison can be done using a variety of methods, which depend in part on the type of indexing used.[1]

---

RAG also reduces the need to retrain LLMs with new data, saving on computational and financial costs.[1] Beyond efficiency gains, RAG also allows LLMs to include sources in their responses, so users can verify the cited sources. This provides greater transparency, as users can cross-check retrieved content to ensure accuracy and relevance.
The term retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) was introduced in a 2020 paper that described combining a parametric language model with a non-parametric external memory accessed through retrieval at inference time.[4]
RAG and LLM limitations

---

Source marker: [Web - Retrieval-augmented generation - Wikipedia]
Retrieval-augmented generation
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a technique that enables large language models (LLMs) to retrieve and incorporate new information from external data sources.[1][2] With RAG, LLMs first refer to a specified set of documents, then respond to user queries. These documents supplement information from the LLM's pre-existing training data.[3] This allows LLMs to use domain-specific and/or updated information that is not available in the training data.[3] For example, this enables LLM-based chatbots to access internal company data or generate responses based on authoritative sources. The technique was first proposed in 2020 and has since become a widely adopted approach in modern AI systems.
RAG improves LLMs by incorporating information retrieval before generating responses.[4] Unlike LLMs that rely on static training data, RAG pulls relevant text from databases, uploaded documents, or web sources.[1] According to Ars Technica, "RAG is a way of improving LLM performance, in essence by blending the LLM process with a web search or other document look-up process to help LLMs stick to the facts." This method helps reduce AI hallucinations,[4] which have caused chatbots to describe policies that don't exist, or recommend nonexistent legal cases to lawyers that are looking for citations to support their arguments.[5]

---

Source marker: [Web - Retrieval-augmented generation - Wikipedia]
The model feeds this relevant retrieved information into the LLM via prompt engineering of the user's original query. Newer implementations (as of 2023[update]) can also incorporate specific augmentation modules with abilities such as expanding queries into multiple domains and using memory and self-improvement to learn from previous retrievals.[citation needed]
Finally, the LLM can generate output based on both the query and the retrieved documents.[3][4] Some models incorporate extra steps to improve output, such as the re-ranking of retrieved information, context selection, and fine-tuning.
Applications
[edit]Retrieval-augmented generation is used in applications where generated responses need to be grounded in external or frequently updated information.[citation needed]
In healthcare, RAG has been studied as a way to ground large language model outputs in external medical knowledge sources, although reviews have noted continuing challenges around evaluation, ethics, and clinical reliability.[8]

Retriever-centric methods
[edit]These methods aim to enhance the quality of document retrieval in vector databases:
- Pre-training the retriever using the Inverse Cloze Task (ICT), a technique that helps the model learn retrieval patterns by predicting masked text within documents.[13]
- Supervised retriever optimization aligns retrieval probabilities with the generator model's likelihood distribution. This involves retrieving the top-k vectors for a given prompt, scoring the generated response's perplexity, and minimizing KL divergence between the retriever's selections and the model's likelihoods to refine retrieval.[14]
- Reranking techniques can refine retriever performance by prioritizing the most relevant retrieved documents during training.[15]
Language model
[edit]By redesigning the language model with the retriever in mind, a 25-time smaller network can get comparable perplexity as its much larger counterparts.[16] Because it is trained from scratch, this method (Retro) incurs the high cost of training runs that the original RAG scheme avoided. The hypothesis is that by giving domain knowledge during training, Retro needs less focus on the domain and can devote its smaller weight resources only to language semantics. answer:
### Summary of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enhances large language models (LLMs) by integrating an information-retrieval mechanism. This allows the models to access and utilize additional data beyond their original training set, enabling them to provide more accurate and up-to-date responses.

### Key Points:

#### How RAG Works:
1. **Embedding Conversion**: Data to be referenced is converted into LLM embeddings, which are numerical representations in a large vector space.
2. **Document Retrieval**: Relevant documents are selected based on the user query using a document retriever.
3. **Prompt Engineering**: The retrieved information is fed into the LLM via prompt engineering of the user's original query.
4. **Response Generation**: The LLM generates output based on both the query and the retrieved documents.

#### Benefits:
1. **Efficiency**: Reduces the need to retrain LLMs with new data, saving computational and financial costs.
2. **Transparency**: Allows LLMs to include sources in their responses, enabling users to verify the cited sources.
3. **Improved Accuracy**: Helps reduce AI hallucinations by grounding responses in external or updated information.

#### Limitations:
1. **Hallucinations**: RAG does not completely prevent LLMs from hallucinating around the source material in their responses.
2. **Evaluation Challenges**: Ongoing challenges in evaluating the effectiveness and reliability of RAG in various applications, particularly in fields like healthcare.
3. **Reproducibility Issues**: Some methods, like Retro, have reproducibility issues, leading to modifications like Retro++.

answer:
### Origin of RAG
RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) was introduced in a 2020 paper that combined a parametric language model with a non-parametric external memory accessed through retrieval at inference time. This technique aims to enhance large language models (LLMs) by allowing them to retrieve and incorporate new information from external data sources.

### Retrieval and Augmentation Process
1. **Data Conversion**: The data to be referenced is converted into LLM embeddings, which are numerical representations in a large vector space.
2. **Storage**: These embeddings are stored in a vector database for efficient document retrieval.
3. **Query Processing**: When a user query is received, a document retriever selects the most relevant documents to augment the query.
4. **LLM Integration**: The LLM then generates output based on both the original query and the retrieved documents.

### Data Sources
RAG can work with various types of data:
- Unstructured data (usually text)
- Semi-structured data
- Structured data (such as knowledge graphs)

### Limitations
1. **Hallucinations**: RAG does not completely prevent LLMs from generating incorrect or misleading information. The LLM can still hallucinate around the source material in its response.
2. **Evaluation Challenges**: Evaluating the effectiveness of RAG remains challenging due to ongoing issues with ethical considerations and clinical reliability.
3. **Contextual Misunderstanding**: LLMs may misinterpret the context of retrieved information, leading to false statements or misinformation.
4. **Poisoning**: RAG systems might retrieve factually correct but misleading sources, leading to errors in interpretation. This can result in the model combining outdated and updated information in a misleading manner.
5. **Uncertainty Handling**: LLMs may struggle to recognize when they lack sufficient information to provide a reliable response, potentially generating answers even when they should indicate uncertainty.

These limitations highlight the need for continued research and improvement in RAG techniques to address these challenges effectively.

answer:
### Weekly Work Limits
- **Maximum Average Working Time:** Mobile drivers must not exceed an average of 48 hours per week over a 26-week reference period. This period can be adjusted to a rolling 26-week period in specific circumstances.
- **Weekly Limit:** There is a maximum of 60 hours of Working Time per week.

### Night Work Limits
- **Night Work Maximum:** No more than 10 hours of night work can be performed within any 24-hour period. Night time is defined as between midnight and 0400 hours for goods vehicles and between 0100 and 0500 hours for passenger vehicles. These limits can be extended in certain circumstances.

### Breaks
- **Rest Periods:** Mobile workers must take a 30-minute break after 6 hours of Working Time and a 45-minute break if they work over 9 hours. Note that EU drivers' hours rules and rest periods still apply.

### Reference Periods
- **26-Week Calendar Reference Period:** The reference period is calculated over a 26-week calendar period. It starts on the nearest Monday on or after 1 April, 1 August, and 1 December, and ends at midnight on the nearest Monday on or after 26 weeks from those dates.
- **Specific Reference Periods:**
  - **Period 1:** From 1 January to 30 June
  - **Period 2:** From 1 July to 31 December

### Employment Responsibilities
- **Informing About Additional Work:** Mobile workers must inform their employer or employment business about any additional Working Time undertaken for other employers or employment businesses during the reference period.
- **Accurate Record Keeping:** Workers are responsible for accurately recording their Working Time during assignments.
- **Compliance:** Non-compliance, such as failing to report other work or making false records, can result in criminal offenses and fines of up to £5,000.

### Declaration Requirements
- **Work Declaration:** Both transport and non-transport work must be declared. Even if some time is excluded from the Working Time calculation, it should still be reported.
- **Charitable/Non-Transport Work:** If engaging in charitable or voluntary work, or work for the Territorial Army (TA), fire service, or police, the worker must inform the employer and declare the time as if it were other work.

These regulations aim to protect the health and safety of mobile workers, other road users, and the public.

RAG can significantly improve answer grounding by incorporating external data sources into the responses generated by large language models (LLMs). This process enhances the accuracy and relevance of the generated content by providing LLMs with up-to-date and domain-specific information. Here’s how RAG supports better answer grounding and verification:

### What RAG Can Do
1. **Incorporate External Data**: RAG allows LLMs to access and integrate information from external sources, such as documents, databases, or web pages. This ensures that the generated responses are grounded in current and relevant data.
2. **Enhance Accuracy**: By referencing specific documents, RAG can help LLMs avoid generating misinformation or hallucinations. Users can verify the cited sources to ensure the accuracy and relevance of the information.
3. **Provide Contextual Information**: RAG can supply detailed contextual information that might not be present in the LLM's pre-existing training data, enriching the responses with nuanced details.

### What RAG Cannot Do
1. **Prevent Hallucinations**: While RAG can reduce the likelihood of hallucinations, it does not completely eliminate them. LLMs can still generate information that is not aligned with the retrieved sources if they misinterpret the context.
2. **Ensure Absolute Reliability**: Even with RAG, there is no guarantee that the retrieved information is always accurate or up-to-date. Sources can contain errors or be outdated.
3. **Address All Knowledge Gaps**: RAG relies on the availability and quality of the external data. If critical information is missing or poorly represented in the retrieved sources, the LLM's responses may still be limited.

### Verification Support
- **Cited Sources**: RAG allows LLMs to include references to the sources used in generating the response. This transparency enables users to verify the information independently.
- **Cross-Checking**: Users can cross-check the retrieved content against other sources to ensure accuracy and relevance.
- **Contextual Understanding**: By providing detailed context from the retrieved sources, RAG helps users understand the basis of the generated information, facilitating better verification.

In summary, RAG enhances answer grounding by integrating external data, but it is not a foolproof solution. Users must remain vigilant and verify the information using the provided sources and independent checks.

[edit]These methods focus on the encoding of text as either dense or sparse vectors. Sparse vectors, which encode the identity of a word, are typically dictionary-length and contain mostly zeros. - Hybrid vector approaches may be used to combine dense vector representations with sparse one-hot vectors, taking advantage of the computational efficiency of sparse dot products over dense vector operations.[9]

Improvements
[edit]Improvements to the basic process above can be applied at different stages in the RAG flow.
Encoder
[edit]These methods focus on the encoding of text as either dense or sparse vectors. Sparse vectors, which encode the identity of a word, are typically dictionary-length and contain mostly zeros. Dense vectors, which encode meaning, are more compact and contain fewer zeros. Various enhancements can improve the way similarities are calculated in the vector stores (databases).[9]
- Performance improves by optimizing how vector similarities are calculated. Dot products enhance similarity scoring, while approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) searches improve retrieval efficiency over K-nearest neighbors (KNN) searches.[10]
- Accuracy may be improved with Late Interactions, which allow the system to compare words more precisely after retrieval. This helps refine document ranking and improve search relevance.[11]
- Hybrid vector approaches may be used to combine dense vector representations with sparse one-hot vectors, taking advantage of the computational efficiency of sparse dot products over dense vector operations.[9]
- Other retrieval techniques focus on improving accuracy by refining how documents are selected. Some retrieval methods combine sparse representations, such as SPLADE, with query expansion strategies to improve search accuracy and recall.[12]

While RAG improves the accuracy of large language models (LLMs), it does not eliminate all challenges. One limitation is that while RAG reduces the need for frequent model retraining, it does not remove it entirely. Additionally, LLMs may struggle to recognize when they lack sufficient information to provide a reliable response. Without specific training, models may generate answers even when they should indicate uncertainty. According to IBM, this issue can arise when the model lacks the ability to assess its own knowledge limitations.[1]
RAG poisoning
[edit]RAG systems may retrieve factually correct but misleading sources, leading to errors in interpretation. In some cases, an LLM may extract statements from a source without considering its context, resulting in an incorrect conclusion. Additionally, when faced with conflicting information, RAG models may struggle to determine which source is accurate. The worst case outcome of this limitation is that the model may combine details from multiple sources producing responses that merge outdated and updated information in a misleading manner. According to the MIT Technology Review, these issues occur because RAG systems may misinterpret the data they retrieve.[3]

RAG and LLM limitations
[edit]LLMs can provide incorrect information. For example, when Google first demonstrated its LLM tool "Bard" (later re-branded to Google Gemini), the LLM provided incorrect information about the James Webb Space Telescope. This error contributed to a $100 billion decline in Google's stock value.[5] RAG is used to prevent these errors, but it does not solve all the problems. For example, LLMs can generate misinformation even when pulling from factually correct sources if they misinterpret the context. MIT Technology Review gives the example of an AI-generated response stating, "The United States has had one Muslim president, Barack Hussein Obama." The model retrieved this from the rhetorical chapter title "Barack Hussein Obama: America's First Muslim President?" in the book Faith in the New Millennium: The Future of Religion and American Politics.[6] The LLM did not "know" or "understand" the context of the title, generating a false statement.[3]
LLMs with RAG are programmed to prioritize new information. This technique has been called "prompt stuffing." Without prompt stuffing, the LLM's input is generated by a user; with prompt stuffing, additional relevant context is added to this input to guide the model's response. This approach provides the LLM with key information early in the prompt, encouraging it to prioritize the supplied data over pre-existing training knowledge.[7]

The model feeds this relevant retrieved information into the LLM via prompt engineering of the user's original query. Newer implementations (as of 2023[update]) can also incorporate specific augmentation modules with abilities such as expanding queries into multiple domains and using memory and self-improvement to learn from previous retrievals.[citation needed]
Finally, the LLM can generate output based on both the query and the retrieved documents.[3][4] Some models incorporate extra steps to improve output, such as the re-ranking of retrieved information, context selection, and fine-tuning.
Applications
[edit]Retrieval-augmented generation is used in applications where generated responses need to be grounded in external or frequently updated information.[citation needed]
In healthcare, RAG has been studied as a way to ground large language model outputs in external medical knowledge sources, although reviews have noted continuing challenges around evaluation, ethics, and clinical reliability.[8]

Retriever-centric methods
[edit]These methods aim to enhance the quality of document retrieval in vector databases:
- Pre-training the retriever using the Inverse Cloze Task (ICT), a technique that helps the model learn retrieval patterns by predicting masked text within documents.[13]
- Supervised retriever optimization aligns retrieval probabilities with the generator model's likelihood distribution. This involves retrieving the top-k vectors for a given prompt, scoring the generated response's perplexity, and minimizing KL divergence between the retriever's selections and the model's likelihoods to refine retrieval.[14]
- Reranking techniques can refine retriever performance by prioritizing the most relevant retrieved documents during training.[15]
Language model
[edit]By redesigning the language model with the retriever in mind, a 25-time smaller network can get comparable perplexity as its much larger counterparts.[16] Because it is trained from scratch, this method (Retro) incurs the high cost of training runs that the original RAG scheme avoided. The hypothesis is that by giving domain knowledge during training, Retro needs less focus on the domain and can devote its smaller weight resources only to language semantics. It has been reported that Retro is not reproducible, so modifications were made to make it so. The more reproducible version is called Retro++ and includes in-context RAG.[17]

RAG also reduces the need to retrain LLMs with new data, saving on computational and financial costs.[1] Beyond efficiency gains, RAG also allows LLMs to include sources in their responses, so users can verify the cited sources. Improvements
[edit]Improvements to the basic process above can be applied at different stages in the RAG flow.
Encoder
[edit]These methods focus on the encoding of text as either dense or sparse vectors. Sparse vectors, which encode the identity of a word, are typically dictionary-length and contain mostly zeros. Dense vectors, which encode meaning, are more compact and contain fewer zeros. Various enhancements can improve the way similarities are calculated in the vector stores (databases).[9]
- Performance improves by optimizing how vector similarities are calculated. Dot products enhance similarity scoring, while approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) searches improve retrieval efficiency over K-nearest neighbors (KNN) searches.[10]
- Accuracy may be improved with Late Interactions, which allow the system to compare words more precisely after retrieval. This helps refine document ranking and improve search relevance.[11]
- Hybrid vector approaches may be used to combine dense vector representations with sparse one-hot vectors, taking advantage of the computational efficiency of sparse dot products over dense vector operations.[9]
- Other retrieval techniques focus on improving accuracy by refining how documents are selected. Some retrieval methods combine sparse representations, such as SPLADE, with query expansion strategies to improve search accuracy and recall.[12]

Retrieval-augmented generation
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a technique that enables large language models (LLMs) to retrieve and incorporate new information from external data sources.[1][2] With RAG, LLMs first refer to a specified set of documents, then respond to user queries. These documents supplement information from the LLM's pre-existing training data.[3] This allows LLMs to use domain-specific and/or updated information that is not available in the training data.[3] For example, this enables LLM-based chatbots to access internal company data or generate responses based on authoritative sources. The technique was first proposed in 2020 and has since become a widely adopted approach in modern AI systems.
RAG improves LLMs by incorporating information retrieval before generating responses.[4] Unlike LLMs that rely on static training data, RAG pulls relevant text from databases, uploaded documents, or web sources.[1] According to Ars Technica, "RAG is a way of improving LLM performance, in essence by blending the LLM process with a web search or other document look-up process to help LLMs stick to the facts." This method helps reduce AI hallucinations,[4] which have caused chatbots to describe policies that don't exist, or recommend nonexistent legal cases to lawyers that are looking for citations to support their arguments.[5]
